To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

finger dexterity declines with age and gender in healthy individuals, but more rapidly in patients with Parkinson's disease and osteoarthritis, and that the dexterity of the legs is also affected by age and gender.
dexterity declines significantly with age in healthy individuals, and that the decline is faster in patients with PD than in patients with OA.

finger dexterity declines with age and is significantly affected by gender, that finger dexterity in patients with osteoarthritis and Parkinson's disease differs from that in healthy individuals, that leg dexterity declines with aging and is significantly affected also by gender, and that leg and finger dexterity are significantly correlated.

the dynamical control of fingertip force vectors during a dynamic manipulation task, which quantifies dexterity.
the neural control of dynamic fingertip forces, and how this control capability is affected by aging and disease.
the dynamical control of unstable systems, and the neural mechanisms that underlie the ability to manipulate such systems in the real world.

finger dexterity declines with age and is affected by gender and disease.
dexterity, as measured by the Strength-Dexterity paradigm, is significantly affected by gender, age, and disease.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

finger dexterity, as measured in the Strength-Dexterity test, depends on gender, age, disease, and limb, and that the temporal variability of force during spring compression provides additional information that can help to distinguish among these factors.

the dexterity of the human hand and foot can be quantified as the dynamical regulation of instabilities, and is affected by gender, age, and disease, and that the dexterity in the hand is strongly correlated with that in the foot.
the neural regulation of fingertip force vectors during dexterous manipulation is a highly complex process, which is influenced by gender, age, disease, and limb dominance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

finger dexterity depends on age, gender, and disease, and that the temporal variability of the forces during the manipulation task may provide a more robust indicator of dexterity than the maximal force.
the ability to dynamically regulate fingertop force vectors and motions is an important component of the dexterity of the human hand and that it is affected by gender, aging and disease.
finger and leg dexterity are quantitatively comparable, suggesting the need to investigate the neural control of both systems in the same individual.
